She spent the weekend knocking on doors.

She did not ask anyone for money. That was the first rule she wrote at the top of her list, and she kept it. She knocked, and when the door opened she said, "My name is Wren Halloway, and I'd like to show you something my father wrote down," and she showed them the page. Their grandmother's crossing. Their father's fuel advance. The night run for the doctor when they were born. Then she told them about the council vote on Monday, and about the pier, and she said, "I'm not asking you for anything. I just thought you should know what the vote is really about." And she went to the next door.

Some of them cried. Some of them shut the door. Old Mr. Gunderson read the 1972 entry three times and then went and got his coat without a word and walked with her to the next house.

By Monday evening, the Saltmarsh Reach town hall was so full that the fire marshal stood at the door counting people with a clicker and gave up at two hundred. They stood along the walls. They sat on the radiators. The fish co-op came in their boots. Prue closed the bakery early and brought her whole kitchen staff. Mrs. Pruitt came in a wheelchair, with her daughter, the one who had been born the night of the 1963 crossing.

Corwin Pell sat in the front row in his camel coat and looked, for the first time since Wren had met him, uncertain.

The rezoning came up fourth on the agenda. Pell's people presented drawings: forty slips, a restaurant, thirty units. Very handsome drawings. Then Marguerite Okafor, the council chair, asked if any member of the public wished to speak, and the room went very quiet, and Wren stood up.

She did not make a speech. She had written one and torn it up. Instead she carried the 1951 ledger to the microphone, and she opened it to the page, and she read the entry out loud. *Crossing, Okafor family, four persons, furniture.* No fare.

Then she sat down.

Mr. Gunderson stood up and read his. Then Mrs. Pruitt's daughter. Then a fisherman Wren barely knew, whose father's boat had been towed home by the *Margaret Ann* in the blizzard of 1978. One after another they stood and read the entries she had copied out for them, forty years of debts nobody had ever been asked to pay, and the room listened in total silence, and Marguerite Okafor took off her glasses and pressed her fingers to her eyes.

The vote was four to one against the rezoning.

Corwin Pell left before the gavel came down. He paused beside Wren's chair on his way out. "You still owe me a hundred and twenty thousand dollars tomorrow, Miss Halloway," he said, quietly, without heat.

"You'll have it," she said, and was astonished to find that she believed it.

Outside, on the town hall steps, in the warm June dark, the fish co-op had already passed a hat. The Gundersons pledged their boat. The Lees at the boatyard offered to carry the note at no interest. By the time the hall emptied, Ada was standing on the bottom step with a clipboard, writing down figures, and the figures had become a cooperative, and the cooperative had a name—the Tidewater Pier Trust—and the name had fifty-six thousand dollars pledged against it before midnight.

And at the bottom of the steps, under the streetlamp, holding a cardboard box with a greasy, rusted, impossible exhaust manifold in it, stood Tobias.

"Dell's cousin in Gloucester," he said. "I drove all night. I didn't ask, I just went." He held out the box. "I figured somebody in this family should learn to ask for things. So I'm asking. Can I come back?"

Wren took the box. It weighed a ton. She set it down on the steps, and then she put her arms around her brother for the first time in ten years, and held on.
